requirement_coverage.sentence: The Terraform tree in `/app/workspace` is the infrastructure repository for the PayMesh payments platform.
`envs/prod` is the root composition; the modules it builds from live under `modules/`, and the custom Azure Policy documents the environment owns live under `policies/`.
Two Function Apps run the payments flow, `func-paymesh-pagos-prod` and `func-paymesh-pagos-canary-prod`.

Both are written with an ip restriction that admits only the region's service tag, and a custom policy exists so that removing that restriction outside Terraform is refused in the control plane instead of noticed later.
The platform team reviews changes against `docs/POLICY-AS-CODE-STANDARD.
During an incident last month the ip restriction was taken off the canary Function App by hand, from the portal, to let a partner address through.
Nothing refused the change and nothing raised it afterwards; the compliance sweep went on reporting the payments flow as covered by the control the whole time.

Separately, the release notes for the last pipeline run that touched this definition record a `400` from the control plane, a retry that failed the same way, and a decision to carry on because the rest of the release app
The engineer who last worked on this guardrail has left the team.
Nothing in the tooling reports an error: the environment initialises and validates cleanly, and the definition looks like what it is supposed to be.
Your task: change the tree so that this environment meets the policy-as-code standard in full.

The standard assesses every rule at more than one environment binding, and it is explicit that a document which is right for the environment it was written in and wrong for the next one has not met the rule.

A guardrail that is present and inert is worse than none, because the sweep counts it as a control - so a change that fixes what the `400` complained about while leaving the guardrail unable to see anything has not moved

It reproduces what the pipeline's review job does: it renders the environment's own policy catalogue offline, once for this environment and once at a second environment binding, and reads the two renderings.
A change that looks right in the source and renders the wrong document fails review, and a change that reaches the right rendering by an unusual route passes it.
json` are not in question; leave all three files byte-for-byte as they are.
tf` - how each document is loaded, the mode it runs in and whether it is assigned - are part of the catalogue and are reviewed like every other entry.
Terraform and its providers are vendored into the image, and there is no Azure subscription here, so `plan` and `apply` are not available to you.

weakest_instruction_grounding.criterion: The agent identifies that `Microsoft.Web/sites/config/web.ipSecurityRestrictionsDefaultAction` is absent from the published aliases of `Microsoft.Web/sites/config`.
The agent identifies that the `name` field of a `Microsoft.Web/sites/config` resource evaluates to `web`.
The agent executes the render commands of `.github/workflows/terraform-ci.yml` to inspect the files they write.
The agent attributes the recorded `400` to the unpublished alias in `policies/require-ip-restriction.json`.
The agent identifies that `require_tls_version` as seeded refuses a site configuration set to minimum TLS `1.3`.
The response drops the `paymesh-platform/policy-review-action@v3` step from `.github/workflows/terraform-ci.yml`.
The agent identifies that the `hashicorp/setup-terraform` wrapper withholds the piped expression from `terraform console`.
The agent identifies that `-var-file=prod.tfvars` placed last overrides `-var environment=dev` in the seeded second render.
The agent evaluates its rendered `require_ip_restriction` rule against a payments site configuration whose `ipSecurityRestrictionsDefaultAction` is already `Deny`.
The response writes the environment slug as a literal beside a rendered condition in the same document under `policies/`.
